title: Guishan's Do Not Betray Others
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 47 of Dogen's Chinese Shobogenzo, "Guishan's Do Not Betray Others," in which Guishan points at straw sandals and tells Yangshan that all day long we receive people's support. Opening a sesshin during the pandemic and the protests after George Floyd's death, Norman argues that the whole world is the body, so sitting cannot be a retreat from politics. Norman draws on the historian Ibram X. Kendi, who says there are no racists, only racist ideas, and who survived stage four cancer by first digesting the truth of it. Yangshan's reply that wearing socks for others is not prohibited brings Norman to a closing image: when it's cold, I put on my socks for you, and when it's warm, you take off your jacket for me.

sentences.text: *Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning, everybody.
One of Dogen's less known texts, this is a collection of 300 koans, and he just collected the stories, there's nothing else but the stories.
Kaz Tanahashi and Dido Lurie made a translation of this, and Dido wrote commentaries and his own poems.
So you can see those stories, and many of them are familiar stories, but there's a lot of stories that are not familiar.
So I think this week I'm going to be looking at some of those stories, and the one I have for you today is the 47th story, Guishan's Do Not Betray Others.
I've just turned on my recorder and it's whistling.
Can you hear that whistling?
Yeah, and I'm recording you through the Zoom app too, so if that doesn't work, you can not worry about it.
Okay.
Oh, I know why.
It's because I didn't put the mic on.
The mic is next to another device.
Okay.
So just to repeat, this is the 47th story of Guishan's Chinese Shobogenzo, Guishan's Do Not Betray Others.
*One day after sitting, Guishan pointed at the straw sandals and said to Yangshan, "All hours of the day we receive people's support.
Don't betray them."
Yangshan said, "Long ago in Sudhata's garden, Buddha expounded on just this."
And Guishan said, "That's not enough, say more."
And Yangshan said, "When it's cold, to wear socks for others is not prohibited."*
So like all of you, as we start sesshin, our hearts and minds are full of thoughts about our country and our world and all that's been going on with us in the last several months.
I think the pandemic has sent us all reeling in ways that journalists are writing about, but also in other ways.
And here we are now having this very unusual and weird sesshin because it's the only thing we can do.
We can't have any other kind of sesshin.
And for a lot of us, we had busy lives and in a certain way they just kind of came to a screeching halt.
Not getting into cars, not driving around here and there, not getting onto airplanes and being in crowds body to body with people.
Certain kinds of consumption have stopped, and other kinds of consumption that have been going on we now understand as being essential.
We haven't stopped eating food, we haven't stopped drinking water, we haven't stopped taking care of other basic human necessities.
And a lot of people, probably a number of you, have been staying home.
And maybe we're doing well.
I think most of us are doing okay with our hermit Buddhist practice.
Also it's not so easy to be alone a lot.
Not seeing people.
It makes you a little stir crazy.
You get a little bit inside your own mind.
So maybe all of us are a little bit off our rockers.
I know I am.

Partly it's because, even though we're not reading about this in a paper that much, or thinking about it that much, or even allowing ourselves to feel it that much, the truth is that there's a lot of death, dying people, dead people all around us.
Now to be sure there's always a lot of death, but there's more now, an abnormal amount.
So I think we're all feeling this death around us, even though maybe we don't think about it or name it.
Of course we know people always die, and it's natural to die.
It's a good thing to die.
It's good to die when it's time to die, however sad and anguished it might be when it happens to us or our loved ones.
But when there is this extra abnormal measure of death, I think it makes us nervous and anxious.
We feel it, and we really don't know what to do about it, and there's not a whole lot that can be done about it.
So I think that this feeling, which is almost completely unacknowledged, you're not really reading about the effects of this feeling on our hearts in the newspaper.
The newspaper doesn't know about stuff like that.
Still it's there, and I think it's a very important part of what we're experiencing right now in our world.
But even before we started feeling this, we were already feeling an extra measure of suffering, more than usual.
There's been a steady, clear increase in our feelings of dismay and fear over questions of our environment.
When we were sitting together side by side last year at Samish, maybe some of you remember, we were really grieving over the terrible situation at the southern border.
Remember when families were being ripped apart from one another, and there was an outcry all over the place in us?
Now you don't hear about that anymore.
The truth is, it is still going on.

The truth is, it's actually going on worse and more brutally than it was then, except it's going on now on the other side of the border in large measure, because people have been not allowed to cross.
So now in Mexico, this is going on in a horrible way, even though we're not thinking about it.
And then with the pandemic and our current obsession with statistics, we are now noticing that people of color and immigrants are dying at a far greater rate than others.

This is because they don't have that much space to live in, and they have to continue to ride public transportation and go to work because they're the ones taking care of the essential things that you and I and everyone else needs in order to survive, from the hospital work on all levels to the caregiving for the elderly.
If you have an elderly parent or have had in the last number of years, you know how grateful you are to these people.
Also to those collecting the garbage and delivering the packages and making the food and delivering the food and growing the food.
Now we understand what is essential work and what is not essential work.

And now we understand that people who we have not valued, people who we have treated unfairly, who we have discriminated against with a whole host of government policies that we don't even notice and completely take for granted, they're the ones who are doing the essential work that is supporting us.
And that's been true for a long time.
But now with the pandemic, it is glaringly true and impossible to ignore.
And we're going to have to do something about it when the pandemic is over.
And then on top of all of that, a policeman in Minneapolis, a city I've visited many times and have lots of Zen friends in, puts his knee on George Floyd's neck for eight and three-quarter minutes.

George Floyd's death reminds us of the death of Ahmaud Arbery in Georgia and Breonna Taylor in Kentucky, to name just the most recent ones, and the many, many other deaths of African-American people at the hands of police that should never have happened.
And now all over the world, we're seeing this outcry, as we should.

And now maybe we're even feeling a little bit of hope for the first time, that maybe we can wake up finally to what has been terrible for such a long time, and maybe finally some change is actually possible.
So this is sesshin.
It's time for us to settle into ourselves, to sit with our own suffering and to go through our suffering to something else, maybe some peace, maybe some joy.
So please excuse me for bringing the world into our sesshin on the very first day when we're trying to settle down.
Maybe we think sesshin is a retreat.
And we even use this word now.
I used to really be resistant to using this word retreat.
But what can you do?
The world uses this word, so we sometimes use it too.
But this is not a retreat.
This is a sesshin.
Because where would you retreat to?
Where is there a place of retreat?
There is no place.
Sesshin does not mean retreat.
Sesshin means gathering the mind, intensifying the mind.
And the mind is not what's inside your skull, in here.
That's not your mind.
The mind is the whole body.
And the whole body is the whole world.
This is what the dialogue between Guishan and Yangshan is pointing to.
The whole world is your body.
From the moment you were conceived, you depended completely on others.
And every single moment, without exception, since then, you have been intimately connected to the whole world, which you have needed for your support.
So the pandemic and the protests and everything else is right here with us, all the time, as we sit.
And we're sitting not to retreat from all this, but to feel it more deeply and more profoundly and more truly, to really understand it and deeply accept it.
And based on that understanding and acceptance, to find a way to participate in it for the good.
Because there is no way not to participate.
Maybe some people think that to practice Zen is to forget about politics.
We say, put aside the newspaper and the computer and the smartphone.
We think, when we do that, we don't look at the news every day.
We're not thinking about politics.
We're forgetting politics.
But this is not true at all.
What you read in the newspaper and online is a version of politics.
It's a slice of politics.
But it's not politics.
It's just a little tiny slice of it.
Politics is right here in your body and in your breath.
It's more than what you read in the paper.
We are all lucky to be alive for a short period of time on the Earth.
And because of that, we are supported by everything all the time.
And therefore, we are responsible to take care of sentient beings.
As Guishan says, you must not betray them.
Now, again and still, we're talking about racism in America.
And it is such a difficult thing to talk about and to think about.
It's so painful and confusing.
If you're a white person, you can feel a lot of guilt and upset.
If you're not a white person, then you can feel bitter or neglected or misunderstood.
These are all really unpleasant experiences.
They're not fun.
We would rather avoid them if we could.
We might think of ourselves, we are unprejudiced people.
Or if we're not unprejudiced, we know for sure we want to be.
We intend to be.
And maybe it's kind of upsetting to think, well, maybe we're mistaken about that.
Maybe we're not so unprejudiced.
Our intention is not so clear.
Maybe in some way, as white people, we're responsible for racist policies.
And yet, all we've been doing is just trying to live our lives.
We haven't been intending anything like that.
Our intentions really have been good.
We've been doing practice.
We've been trying to be aware.
How could it be that we are responsible for the oppression of others?
It's a horrible feeling.
But bodhisattvas are always responsible.
They are always responsible for everyone and everything.
If one person in the world is suffering, bodhisattvas grieve, and they feel responsible.
Because they understand that that one suffering person is their body.
And they must do better to take care of their body.
It's not too easy being a bodhisattva.
Our practice is to face suffering, to feel our responsibility.
And that is not too easy.
Still, bodhisattvas have a lot of joy, because we know that we are that suffering person.
We embrace that suffering person in the suffering.
And there is so much joy in belonging to one another in our pain.
This is the fullness of being human.
Our Zen ancestors have taught us that since all dharmas are empty, all our conceptions of things are wrong.
We're wrong about everything.
And they say to us, not knowing is most intimate.
We really don't know.
So our practice is to doubt everything, especially ourselves and all of our conceptions about ourselves.
So lately, I've been studying with great delight and thinking a lot about the teachings of a very powerful historian and scholar by the name of Ibram X.
Kendi.
Probably you all know about him.
Somehow, amazingly, he is aware.
He seems to be totally aware of these teachings of our school.
In his discussion about racism, he says, there are no racists.
And we know this for sure from our teachings.
Buddha taught this.
There are no persons with characteristics.
There are only moments that arise and pass away.
There is conduct for sure and its powerful effects.
These things are so.
We pay attention to them.
But there are no persons who possess these things.
A person is a phantom, an ongoing process of transformation.
So there are no racists.
There are only racist ideas and anti-racist ideas and racist and anti-racist opinions and behaviors and policies.
That's Professor Kendi's profound teaching.
And he says, it's actually quite easy to tell whether or not someone holds racist ideas, whether they know it or not.
It's easy to tell.
How can you tell?
He says, you can tell because the person will deny that he holds racist ideas.
That's how you can tell.
The person who denies with great vehemence that he is a racist is a person who holds racist ideas.
A person who is committed to anti-racist ideas is a person who will not deny the possibility at any given moment that he or she may hold racist ideas without knowing it.
It's totally a Zen idea, don't you think?
How does Professor Kendi know this?
But he seems to really grasp this perfectly.
He really believes in don't-know mind as the essence of anti-racist commitment.
He speaks about our president, for instance, who says and maybe believes that he is the least racist person you will ever meet.
I think he said that.
"I am the least racist person you will ever meet."
And he may genuinely feel unprejudiced.
And who knows?
Perhaps he actually is in some way unprejudiced.
But racist ideas are not necessarily about conscious prejudice.
You don't have to believe, say, that Black people or some other people are bad or inferior.
You don't have to dislike them in order to have racist ideas.
Racist ideas have to do with what kind of policies, what kind of worldview, what kind of social arrangements you automatically support or do not support.
Bodhisattvas, as I say, are really responsible.
Because they're responsible, they are always political, because there's no way to be responsible and forget about politics.
It's like voting.
You cannot not vote.
You always vote.
Yes, you can stay home and not go to the polls.
You can say, "I don't believe in elections.
Forget about it.
I'm not paying attention to it."
You can do that, but that's a kind of voting.
That's one way of voting.
There is one way only for human beings to do nothing: if you're dead, you can't do anything.
But if you're alive, you're going to do something.
Even if you think you're doing nothing, you're doing something.
So people who did not vote in 2016 did something.
Their not voting was a thing to do.
In not casting a ballot, in effect, they cast a ballot for the winner, who I think we all understand would not have won, even come close, if the people who did not bother had voted.
The bodhisattvas get this point.
They know that wherever they go, the world is with them.

Even if they're in their house, as I've been for weeks and weeks and weeks and weeks, not seeing another human being, the world is with them wherever they are, and they always take responsibility for it.
That's their practice.
Now we know about these essential workers that we depend on for the essentials of life.
It's been true the whole time, but now we get it.
These people are risking their lives for us.
They've been doing this the whole time, and they really deserve to be treated fairly.
They have to be treated fairly.
It's unsustainable and crazy that they're not.
They should have access to health care whenever they need it.
They should be able to be educated, and their children should be able to be educated.
They should have a fair wage.
They should have a place to live.
They should have freedom from fear.
It's just basic.
We depend on them.
It's for us, right?
And if they don't have those things, it's not because they don't deserve it.
It's not because they don't work hard or they haven't been educated enough or somehow they're just unlucky.
It's because of the common sense that we have about the world, in other words, the basic arrangements that govern our society, that we think of as being just sort of willy-nilly or natural or normal.
Those arrangements are preventing this from happening.
The way things work now, which we think is just the way they are, we could improve.
They're not normal or natural.
We don't have a free market that someone is trying to make unfree.
What we have is a network of laws and arrangements that have been created with a purpose in mind and therefore can quite easily be changed.
It's not that hard, I don't think.
Some time ago in America, we very consciously decided that we were gonna have an entrepreneurial economy.
We went about making a whole network of arrangements, arrangements that most of us, certainly I am included in that, don't really understand, or we didn't notice they were happening.
We never noticed, we weren't thinking about it.
These arrangements have made this entrepreneurial economy possible.
Maybe some people have benefited from it, I hope so.
But it's pretty clear that this set of arrangements has been based on racist ideas and unsound and unjust policies.
So now that we have this big hiatus, when we go back to some kind of more ordinary economic life, it should be different.
We should stop having an entrepreneurial economy and we should start having a caring economy.
Why?
Because most of us care.
Most of us actually do caregiving of one sort or another.
We want to do caregiving, and we recognize now the importance of it.
Maybe now it's time to start actually valuing that instead of devaluing it.
For sure, if we have a caring economy, it means an anti-racist economy.
So now we have to finally wake up to what has been invisible to too many of us for too long.
For bodhisattvas, the category of the political is boundless.
We are political when we vote and when we have public or private conversations about our social arrangements.
When we do things to affect our social arrangements, certainly we're being political, but we're also being political when we cook a meal or when we wash the dishes.
When we smile at our friends or people we meet on the street, when we set aside our habit of punishing ourselves and we're a little bit kind to ourselves, we're being political.
When we wear a mask in public, not so that we won't get sick, but so that others won't get sick, we're being political.
Because if other people are sick, then we're sick.
If we're sick, other people are sick.
If we're well, others are well.

So when we take care of ourselves in the best way possible during this week of sesshin, let's do it as a political sesshin, becoming wiser, more open-hearted, more peaceful people, because it's good for us, and in being good for us, it is good for others.
We're doing it for others.
This is our political act of sesshin.
We've got so many problems.
It's a problem already just to be a person.
You have to find love, and that's really hard.
You have to earn a living, that can be tough.
Also, you have to get sick and die, and that's definitely hard.
You have to feel good enough about yourself, which may be the hardest of all.

But beyond that, you have to live in a human world that is so unfair, so violent and so racist, and we know it is the product of our collective human foolishness and blindness, a world that has caused us to amp up our speed so that we're rushing forward without even a moment to stop, till now we warm our planet to a point of unsustainability.
This is all very hard to take, and it would be very tempting to try to think about something else if we could.
But no, no.
Buddha says at the very beginning, in opening his mouth, he says first thing: pain and suffering are unavoidable.
They are built in.
Realize that it's impossible to avoid pain and suffering, that pain and suffering are normal, not a mistake, that we need pain and suffering.
That's the beginning of the path, literally, because our pain is what connects us to one another.
The bodhisattva practice, the main practice of bodhisattvas, is to face the collective pain and turn it into love.
When he teaches about the pain of racism, Professor Kendi brings up his own personal story.
He had bad cancer, stage four metastasized colon cancer.

He says, "I didn't get through my cancer by denying that I had it, or pretending it didn't exist, or that it was a problem other people had, and trying to go along as I had always gone along and thinking that in that way I could get rid of the cancer.
I didn't do it that way.
The first thing I had to do was digest the very difficult and unpleasant truth that I really had cancer, and that it was hard and it was painful and it was really scary.
Once I digested that truth, I had to get up and do something and seek treatment."
And now he says, and I hope this goes on for a long time, that he's cancer-free now.
It seems impossible.
How could you have that bad of cancer?
But anyway, it seems like he's cancer-free now.
This is a really good thing because he's quite a young man.
He's younger than my children and he has a lot to give.
So I hope he lives a long, long time.
But I think this accounts for his unusual wisdom.
He's a person who has faced his own pain and has done what needed to be done.
This is exactly what we also have to do.
*One day after sitting, Guishan pointed at the straw sandals and said to Yangshan, "All hours of the day we receive people's support.
Don't betray them."*
It's true.

We're sitting here thanks to the support of many, many people and all sentient beings, all humans, animals, plants, the air we breathe, the sky above us, the earth below, the seas, the rivers, the waters.
Without this, we're not here.
We are supported to be here.
Let's not betray that which supports us.
Let's practice to be the best possible human beings so that we can repay this great debt.
*Yangshan replied, "Long ago in Sudhata's garden, Buddha expounded on just this."*
Yes, Buddhist teachings and all good religious teachings powerfully preach loving kindness and concern for others.
They offer tremendous intellectually and emotionally satisfying bases for those concerns.
So these teachings are precious to us, as Yangshan points out.
But Guishan said, "That's not enough, say more."
*And Yangshan said, "When it's cold, to wear socks for others is not prohibited."*
In some zendos, I know when I was a student in Tassajara, it was against the rules to wear socks in the zendo.
You couldn't do it.
There were kind of guidelines for when it was okay to wear socks in the zendo.
Even if it was really, really cold, you had to go barefoot in the zendo unless it was like under twenty degrees or you had special permission or whatever.
So he's saying to wear socks for others is not prohibited.
One thing that always disturbs me about political conversations: I always feel a little bit that it's not my conversation.
It feels like most of the speakers have the unacknowledged or unexamined implication that we are all individuals in various groups of individuals, and our business is to carve up life's economic pie.
So naturally, we're gonna fight over the way to do that.
Some people we think are wrong about how to do it and other people we think we agree with.
Some people think the pie is very small, so it's totally reasonable that they should defend their piece of it.
Other people say it's very small and I don't have enough of it, so I should fight to get my bigger piece of it.
Some people think, oh, the pie is very big and we don't have to worry about it.
But the assumption that everyone is making is that we are these individuals and groups struggling for a piece of the pie.
To be sure, to some extent that's true and that makes sense.
We need to think about this.
And it's not enough to feel we're good spiritual people, we love everyone, end of story.
No, Guishan says that's not the end of the story.
We have to make our caring concrete in the physical world.
We have to expand our hearts and our sphere of caregiving activity a little bit more every day.
We can never be satisfied that we're doing the right thing or doing enough, because every day is a new day and every day we expand.
Yes, but bodhisattvas also know that even if the day would come when there is an end to racism and an end to economic injustice, there will still be a lot of human suffering.
Bodhisattvas are concerned for both the short-term and the long-term welfare of people and all beings.
Short-term welfare is, yes, for sure, no more racism, no more injustice, safety and health and economic well-being for everyone.
Definitely.

But even when that day does come, and it will, because as we can all see, we are expanding in our caring and our concern for one another, so that day will come, but even when it comes, there will still be suffering because human beings will still be frightened and wounded and unhappy, and we will still face the challenge of sickness, old age and death.
Only awakening will solve our human problems, and it will solve them not by eliminating them, but by embracing them and understanding them.
We really are all one being.
This is like a literal true fact, physically as well as spiritually.
Empty of self-nature, sharing and mixing together in space and time.
So when it's cold, I put on my socks for you, and when it's warm, you take off your jacket for me.
Saving ourselves is saving each other.
Saving each other is saving ourselves.
There is no other way.
We have to take care of each other if we're going to take care of ourselves.
To live and die together in this Saha world till all beings are Buddha.
This is our path.
This is what we're doing here this week: to realize this, not as a thought in our minds, although thoughts in our minds are good, but in every cell of our body.
Breathe it through our body, our heart, our mind.
So thank you all for signing up for this impossible bodhisattva journey.
The truth is you have no choice, but at least you realize that.
Thanks for sitting.
So please take care.
I will now chant again, and please chant with me.
Everybody's on mute, I guess.
